W4 • Assessment in Teaching

Four Assessment Types: From Evidence to Action

Effective assessment connects knowledge to practice: identify a starting point, provide feedback, evaluate learning, and give students opportunities to apply what they know.

Before learningDuring learningAfter learningReal-world transfer
Teaching perspective: Interactive lessons can combine short knowledge checks, flashcards, decision-based scenarios, practical tasks, and evidence checks. Each assessment type reveals something different about student learning.
01 • Before instruction

Pre-assessment

What do students already know and need?

Three key points

  1. An initial knowledge check distinguishes familiar vocabulary from concepts students can explain or perform.
  2. Questions about prerequisites and common terms can expose gaps before a challenging lesson begins.
  3. Results can guide pacing and differentiated support rather than count as a final achievement grade.

Applications in a future classroom

  • Before a technology lesson, students could identify tools and explain the order of basic setup steps; responses would guide small-group support.
  • Before a decision-making unit, a brief ungraded prompt about evidence, limitations, and responsible choices could reveal misconceptions.
02 • During instruction

Formative assessment

How can learning improve right now?

Three key points

  1. Brief checks during a lesson show whether students understand the reasoning, not just whether they completed the activity.
  2. Specific feedback is useful when it explains why a choice worked or what should be reconsidered (Hattie & Timperley, 2007).
  3. Assessment evidence becomes formative when teachers or students use it to improve the next learning step (Black & Wiliam, 1998).

Applications in a future classroom

  • Students could use flip-style review cards and “practice again / understood” self-checks to decide which ideas need more study.
  • During a hands-on task, students could check an observable result after each step and use feedback to correct errors before continuing.
03 • At a learning milestone

Summative assessment

What has been learned?

Three key points

  1. At the end of a learning sequence, summative evidence indicates whether students met the stated objectives.
  2. Final assessments should match the target: knowledge may be assessed through questions, while a procedure may require demonstration.
  3. Scores summarize achievement, while patterns of mistakes can inform future instruction.

Applications in a future classroom

  • At the end of a unit on evidence-based decisions, students could complete a short knowledge check scored against clear learning criteria.
  • For a technology unit, students could demonstrate a complete setup sequence using an outcome-based checklist rather than only answering multiple-choice questions.
04 • Learning in context

Authentic assessment

Can students use learning in realistic situations?

Three key points

  1. Realistic challenges ask students to apply knowledge to situations where decisions and outcomes matter (Wiggins, 1990).
  2. Students interpret information, make choices, and justify decisions rather than rely on recall alone.
  3. A rubric can assess reasoning, accuracy, and verification of the final result.

Applications in a future classroom

  • A “Learn → Do → Verify → Troubleshoot” activity could ask students to complete a practical setup challenge, document results, and explain corrections.
  • A scenario-based task could ask students to weigh competing evidence, consider limitations, and defend a recommendation with a clear rationale.

How the four approaches work together

Diagnose→Respond→Evaluate→Transfer

For a technology or problem-solving unit, begin with a prerequisite check (pre-assessment), use flashcards and step-by-step feedback during practice (formative), evaluate unit goals with a final demonstration or quiz (summative), and assign a realistic scenario that requires verified results and a justified decision (authentic).

Discussion question

How might you adapt a “Learn → Do → Verify → Troubleshoot” sequence to your own classroom, and where would you place feedback before the final assessment?

Authentic tasks may also be formative or summative; their purpose depends on when the evidence is collected and how it is used.

References

  1. Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (1998). Assessment and classroom learning. Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice, 5(1), 7–74. https://doi.org/10.1080/0969595980050102
  2. Hattie, J., & Timperley, H. (2007). The power of feedback. Review of Educational Research, 77(1), 81–112. https://doi.org/10.3102/003465430298487
  3. Wiggins, G. (1990). The case for authentic assessment. Practical Assessment, Research & Evaluation, 2(2). https://doi.org/10.7275/ffb1-mm19
